title: Aadhaar eSign in Django: send PDFs for signature and verify webhooks
author: Atul Thakur
summary: Indian businesses run on signed PDFs: rent agreements, offer letters, NDAs, loan sanction letters. Aadhaar eSign lets a signer sign with an OTP sent to their Aadhaar-linked mobile, and the result is a valid electronic signature under Section 3A of the IT Act 2000. No printer, no courier, no USB token. This tutorial adds Aadhaar eSign to a Django project using the SignYu API . SignYu sits in front of a licensed eSign provider (eMudhra), so you work with a plain REST API and webhooks instead of gateway encryption and redirects. By the end you will have: A Contract model that tracks each document. A view that uploads a PDF, adds signers, and sends it. A webhook view that verifies the HMAC signature and updates the model. A view that downloads the completion certificate. There is also a Django guide at signyu.com/aadhaar-esign-api/integrations/django . Prerequisites Python 3.9+ and Django 4.2+ (the code also works on Django 5). A SignYu account with API access: ₹999/month with a 3-day free trial, and each signature uses one credit (₹15 per signature on packs of 10 or more, GST included). Create an API key under Developers at https://signyu.com/app/developers . There is no sandbox, because every signature is a real Aadhaar eSign. Use your own phone for testing and keep a few credits aside. 1. Install and configure pip install signyu Keep secrets in environment variables, not in settings.py : export SIGNYU_API_KEY = sk_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx export SIGNYU_WEBHOOK_SECRET = your_endpoint_signing_secret # config/settings.py import os SIGNYU_API_KEY = os . environ [ " SIGNYU_API_KEY " ] SIGNYU_WEBHOOK_SECRET = os . environ [ " SIGNYU_WEBHOOK_SECRET " ] Create a small module that builds the client once per process: # contracts/signyu_client.py from functools import lru_cache from django.conf import settings from signyu import SignYu @lru_cache ( maxsize = 1 ) def get_client () -> SignYu : return SignYu ( api_key = settings . SIGNYU_API_KEY , timeout = 60.0 ) 2. A model to track documents Store SignYu's documentId so webhooks can find the right row. # contracts/models.py from django.conf import settings from django.db import models class Contract ( models . Model ): class Status ( models . TextChoices ): PENDING = " PENDING " SENT = " SENT " COMPLETED = " COMPLETED " owner = models . ForeignKey ( settings . AUTH_USER_MODEL , on_delete = models . CASCADE ) title = models . CharField ( max_length = 200 ) signyu_document_id = models . CharField ( max_length = 64 , unique = True ) status = models . CharField ( max_length = 16 , choices = Status . choices , default = Status . PENDING ) signed_count = models . PositiveSmallIntegerField ( default = 0 ) completed_at = models . DateTimeField ( null = True , blank = True ) created_at = models . DateTimeField ( auto_now_add = True ) def __str__ ( self ) -> str : return f " { self . title } ( { self . status } ) " python manage.py makemigrations contracts && python manage.py migrate 3. Send a PDF for signature Three API calls: create the document (multipart PDF upload, up to 10MB), add signers (up to 6), and send. Phone numbers must be digits only, at least 10. # contracts/forms.py from django import forms class SendContractForm ( forms . Form ): title = forms . CharField ( max_length = 200 ) file = forms . FileField () signer_name = forms . CharField ( max_length = 120 ) signer_phone = forms . RegexField ( regex = r " ^\d{10,}$ " , help_text = " Digits only " ) signer_email = forms . EmailField () def clean_file ( self ): f = self . cleaned_data [ " file " ] if f . content_type != " application/pdf " : raise forms . ValidationError ( " Upload a PDF. " ) if f . size > 10 * 1024 * 1024 : raise forms . ValidationError ( " PDF must be 10MB or smaller. " ) return f # contracts/views.py from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required from django.shortcuts import redirect , render from signyu import SignYuError from .forms import SendContractForm from .models import Contract from .signyu_client import get_client @login_required def send_contract ( request ): form = SendContractForm ( request . POST or None , request . FILES or None ) if request . method == " POST " and form . is_valid (): data = form . cleaned_data upload = data [ " file " ] client = get_client () try : doc = client . documents . create ( file = upload . read (), file_name = upload . name , name = data [ " title " ], ) client . documents . add_signers ( doc [ " documentId " ], [{ " name " : data [ " signer_name " ], " phone " : data [ " signer_phone " ], " email " : data [ " signer_email " ], }]) # Deducts one credit per signer and emails each signer a link. sent = client . documents . send ( doc [ " documentId " ]) except SignYuError as err : # err.code examples: insufficient_credits, invalid_request, file_too_large form . add_error ( None , f " { err . message } ( { err . code } ) " ) else : Contract . objects . create ( owner = request . user , title = data [ " title " ], signyu_document_id = sent [ " documentId " ], status = Contract . Status . SENT , ) return redirect ( " contracts:list " ) return render ( request , " contracts/send.html " , { " form " : form }) The template only needs enctype="multipart/form-data" : <!-- contracts/templates/contracts/send.html --> <form method= "post" enctype= "multipart/form-data" > {% csrf_token %} {{ form.as_p }} <button type= "submit" > Send for Aadhaar eSign </button> </form> Two things worth knowing: Call send once per document. It charges credits for every signer. If a request times out, look the document up with client.documents.get(document_id) before you try again. sent["signers"][i]["signUrl"] is the same link SignYu emails. You can also show it in your UI or send it over SMS or WhatsApp yourself. For long uploads you may prefer to move these calls into a Celery or RQ task. The code is the same. 4. Verify and handle webhooks SignYu posts two events to your endpoint: Event When signer.signed One signer finished document.completed All signers finished Each request has an X-SignSetu-Event header and an X-SignSetu-Signature header of the form sha256=<hex> , the HMAC-SHA256 of the raw request body keyed with your endpoint's signing secret. (The headers keep the product's former name, SignSetu.) In Django the raw bytes are request.body . Never verify against json.loads(...) re-serialized output. Webhooks come from SignYu's servers, not a browser, so the view must be CSRF exempt. The HMAC check replaces CSRF protection. # contracts/webhooks.py import signyu from django.conf import settings from django.http import HttpResponse , HttpResponseBadRequest from django.utils.dateparse import parse_datetime from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt from django.views.decorators.http import require_POST from .models import Contract @csrf_exempt @require_POST def signyu_webhook ( request ): try : event = signyu . webhooks . construct_event ( request . body , # raw bytes request . headers . get ( " X-SignSetu-Signature " ), settings . SIGNYU_WEBHOOK_SECRET , ) except signyu . WebhookSignatureError : return HttpResponseBadRequest ( " Invalid signature " ) contract = Contract . objects . filter ( signyu_document_id = event [ " documentId " ]). first () if contract is None : # Not ours (or created outside this app). Acknowledge so it is not retried. return HttpResponse ( " ok " ) signed = sum ( 1 for s in event [ " signers " ] if s [ " hasSigned " ]) if event [ " event " ] == " signer.signed " : # Idempotent: only move the counter forward. Contract . objects . filter ( pk = contract . pk , signed_count__lt = signed ). update ( signed_count = signed ) elif event [ " event " ] == " document.completed " : Contract . objects . filter ( pk = contract . pk ). update ( status = Contract . Status . COMPLETED , signed_count = signed , completed_at = parse_datetime ( event [ " completedAt " ]) if event . get ( " completedAt " ) else None , ) return HttpResponse ( " ok " ) If you would rather not depend on the SDK for this, the standard library is enough: import hashlib import hmac from typing import Optional def verify ( raw_body : bytes , header : Optional [ str ], secret : str ) -> bool : if not header : return False expected = " sha256= " + hmac . new ( secret . encode (), raw_body , hashlib . sha256 ). hexdigest () return hmac . compare_digest ( expected , header ) Wire up the URLs: # contracts/urls.py from django.urls import path from . import views , webhooks app_name = " contracts " urlpatterns = [ path ( " send/ " , views . send_contract , name = " send " ), path ( " <int:pk>/certificate/ " , views . certificate , name = " certificate " ), path ( " webhooks/signyu/ " , webhooks . signyu_webhook , name = " signyu-webhook " ), ] Then in the SignYu dashboard under Developers , add https://your-domain.com/contracts/webhooks/signyu/ , copy the signing secret into SIGNYU_WEBHOOK_SECRET , and enable the endpoint. For local testing, run cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8000 (or ngrok) and register that HTTPS URL. Add the tunnel host to ALLOWED_HOSTS . Handler rules: return a 2xx quickly (non-2xx or a 10 second timeout triggers retries with backoff), and keep the handler idempotent, because an event can be delivered more than once. 5. Download the completion certificate Once a contract is complete, the certificate endpoint returns a PDF with a Signature Completion Certificate and a chronological audit trail of the signing events. client.documents.get(id)["downloadUrl"] gives a short-lived link to the signed PDF itself. # contracts/views.py (continued) from django.http import Http404 , HttpResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 @login_required def certificate ( request , pk ): contract = get_object_or_404 ( Contract , pk = pk , owner = request . user ) if contract . status != Contract . Status . COMPLETED : raise Http404 ( " Not signed yet " ) pdf = get_client (). documents . get_certificate ( contract . signyu_document_id ) response = HttpResponse ( pdf , content_type = " application/pdf " ) response [ " Content-Disposition " ] = f ' attachment; filename= " certificate- { pk } .pdf "' return response Requesting it before completion returns 409 invalid_state , which the SDK raises as SignYuError . Production checklist API key only in environment variables or a secrets manager. If it leaks, delete it in the dashboard to revoke it immediately. Gate send_contract behind login and your own permissions; it spends credits. Show a clear message on 402 insufficient_credits . Retry 429 and 5xx with backoff; do not retry other 4xx errors. Drive status from webhooks, and reconcile occasionally with client.documents.list() . Wrapping up That is a complete Django integration: a model, a send view, a verified webhook, and a certificate download. The full API reference (including custom signature placement per page) is in the SignYu docs , with an OpenAPI spec and a Postman collection . The Django guide is at signyu.com/aadhaar-esign-api/integrations/django , and if part of your stack is JavaScript, see the Next.js guide or my Next.js version of this tutorial . The Python SDK used here is open source at github.com/SignYu/signyu-python . Disclosure: I work on SignYu (formerly SignSetu).

title: Five things to know before you build on the USAJOBS Search API
author: Your Evenings Data
summary: USAJOBS publishes an official Search API ( data.usajobs.gov/api/Search ) for US federal job announcements. We built a scheduled job feed on it, and these are the details that shaped the code. Disclosure: the hosted version at the end is ours, and we charge for it. 1. Pay comes with an interval code Each pay range comes with a RateIntervalCode : PA for per year, PH for per hour, plus PD , PW , BW and PM for daily, weekly, biweekly and monthly. To compare jobs on salary, convert everything to a yearly figure. We use 2,087 hours for a year of hourly pay (the federal standard), 260 days, 52 weeks, 26 pay periods or 12 months. Filter on the top of the range, or you'll drop hourly jobs that pay well. 2. One query stops at 10,000 results The API won't page past 10,000 results for one query. A broad search such as "all jobs posted this month" can hit that limit without telling you. Narrow it by location, agency, occupational series or a posted-within window, and log it whenever a query reaches the limit, so a short result is never mistaken for a complete one. 3. Ask for public jobs explicitly Many announcements are open only to current federal employees or particular groups. If your users are the general public, request WhoMayApply=Public . It's also the only option the API serves to a key that hasn't been given extra authorisation. 4. Codes need a lookup table Schedule, appointment, service type and travel come back as codes. Map them to words (Full-time, Permanent, Competitive, Occasional travel) before anyone downstream sees them, or every consumer ends up writing their own mapping. 5. Announcements contain contact details Rows can carry an agency contact email and phone number, and the announcement text can include more of them, sometimes with a named person. Unless your use case needs them, drop the contact fields and mask emails and phone numbers in free text. Don't store full announcement text by default. The hosted version (disclosure: we built it) Our Apify Actor, Government Jobs API: USAJOBS , does all five for you: Yearly pay is worked out for every row with a standard pay interval, and the salary filter runs before you're charged. A free scan_limit row tells you when a search hit the 10,000 limit. Public jobs only , with codes turned into words. Contact details are dropped and masked by default. No API key is needed on your side. Monitor mode returns only jobs it hasn't returned before. Pricing: $0.002 per job, plus $0.01 for a monitor run that finds new jobs (base prices; higher Apify plans pay less). { "keywords" : [ "data scientist" ], "locations" : [ "Washington, District of Columbia" ], "radiusMiles" : 25 , "postedWithinDays" : 14 , "minSalaryUsd" : 100000 } Not an official USAJOBS or OPM product, and not endorsed by any federal agency. Always check the official announcement on usajobs.gov before you apply.

title: I held a séance for a feature that lived 17 minutes
author: TaseenTariq
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built On 30 September, at 15:07:58, I gave my Android app TapOff a new trick: turn the phone on its side, tap the camera hole, and the brightness and volume sliders open. At 15:25:05 I deleted it. Seventeen minutes and seven seconds. About the camera tap, the commit that killed it says only "Removed the lock-screen double-tap switch and the landscape camera tap, with their code". The rest of the story is in the code that died. One comment in it explains the whole thing: in portrait, Android's status bar sits over the camera and takes every tap there. So the trick only ever worked sideways, and I asked for it to go. Every project has a graveyard like this, and nobody visits it. So for Día de los Muertos I built Exhume : a medium that runs on my laptop, digs up the dead, and lets me ask them what happened. Exhume knows three graveyards: Code: files and functions deleted from a git repo, read from its history. Websites: dead sites, read back from the Wayback Machine. My demo is Orkut. Apps: Mac apps I stopped opening, from the last-opened date macOS keeps. For each one it does the same three things: Finds the dead and collects the evidence: commits, dates, authors, archived pages. Each piece gets an ID (E1, E2, …). The facts (when it was born, when it died, who made it, how long it lived) are worked out by code, not by the model. Writes a tombstone: a cause of death and an epitaph, written by Gemma from that evidence only. Holds a séance: you ask questions, and every answer cites the evidence it rests on. Under each answer Exhume prints the sentence from that evidence that backs it up, so you can check it yourself. If the evidence doesn't say, the answer is "The spirits are silent." Here's the camera tap, summoned: $ python3 exhume.py summon cameraTap "Why only in landscape?" The code that was removed included a comment stating that the camera tap was for landscape only because in portrait the status bar sits over the camera and takes every tap there. [E5] E5: // Tapping the camera, in landscape only: in portrait the status bar sits over the camera and takes every tap there. And here's what happens when the evidence has nothing to say. EdgeVolume was a TapOff file that lived 46 minutes; the commit that added it called it "untested on device yet". $ python3 exhume.py summon EdgeVolume "How many people downloaded you?" The spirits are silent. Then I pointed it at a bigger grave: Orkut, Google's first social network. The oldest copy of orkut.com in the Wayback Machine is from 2 February 2001, three years before Orkut opened. In 2003 its title was "Web Page Under Construction". Orkut itself ran from January 2004 to September 2014, says the archive page Google left behind. $ python3 exhume.py summon orkut "When did you die?" I was bid farewell in June 2014, and the service was set to shut down on September 30, 2014. [E4] E4: We will shut down Orkut on September 30, 2014. Asked how many users it had, Orkut's spirit said "over 300 million" and cited E7. E7 isn't Google: it's the page the founder, the engineer orkut.com was named after, put up at orkut.com in 2016. So the number is his own claim, and the citation is what tells you so. The apps graveyard is the smallest. find apps --days 14 found one app I'd stopped opening, NordVPN, last opened on 7 October. Its tombstone's cause of death reads "The record does not say why." That's the right answer: macOS knows when, not why. Demo The full 58-second video, with sound and captions: exhume.tech/demo.mp4 . The terminal scenes are real runs of the same exhume.py that's on GitHub, replayed on screen with Gemma's waits sped up; the real time each call took is shown. The live site: exhume.tech . It tells the camera tap's story as a scrolling comic, with the real evidence behind each grave one click away. Every answer in this post is copied from a real run on my Mac. Code taseen-t / exhume A local Gemma medium for three graveyards: deleted code, dead websites and unused Mac apps. Every answer cites its evidence. Exhume Talk to the dead, on your own laptop. Exhume is a medium that runs Gemma 4 locally through Ollama. It lets you question three kinds of dead things: code deleted from a git repository, websites that now live only in the Wayback Machine, and Mac apps you stopped opening. Live: exhume.tech · Code: this repo · Agent session: Entire checkpoint Every graveyard works the same way: Find the dead. Code collects the evidence, numbers each piece (E1, E2, …) and works out the facts itself: dates, commits, authors, how long it lived. Tombstone. Gemma writes the cause of death and an epitaph, from the evidence only. Summon. Ask it anything. Every answer cites the evidence it rests on. When the evidence doesn't say, the answer is "The spirits are silent." Verify in 30 seconds Model Gemma 4 E4B ( gemma4:e4b ), run locally with Ollama. Licence: Apache 2.0 . … View on GitHub How I Built It Model: Gemma 4 E4B ( gemma4:e4b , open weights, Apache 2.0), running locally through Ollama's HTTP API. No cloud model is called. Code: one Python file, exhume.py , 723 lines, standard library only. It calls git, curl and macOS's mdls . No frameworks, nothing to pip install . Code graveyard: git log -M --diff-filter=D finds deleted files that never came back. For functions, Exhume walks the whole history ( git log -p -M --unified=0 ) and matches definition lines in common languages. That's a heuristic, not a parser. Renamed files don't count, and neither does a function that comes back in the same place under a new name. Binary files are skipped, and --skip GLOB ignores generated folders. On TapOff it found 8 graves. Website graveyard: the Wayback Machine's CDX index lists the saved copies of the home page, and Exhume reads four of them, spread across the years; --page adds snapshots you name. For Orkut that's 8 pages: four home pages (2003, 2008, 2023, 2026) plus four I picked (Google's June 2014 goodbye post, the archive notice, the "Preserving Orkut's history" post and the founder's 2016 page). Pages are cached on disk, so once find has run, tombstones and séances work offline. Apps graveyard: mdls reads kMDItemLastUsedDate for each app in /Applications . Apps macOS has no record of opening are left out unless you ask for them with --unrecorded . Apps only, never documents. Keeping Gemma honest: Gemma never supplies a date, a commit or a name. Code gives it the evidence as a numbered list in the prompt. Gemma must answer in JSON that matches a schema (Ollama's format ). Its cites list is an enum of that grave's real evidence IDs, and code drops anything else anyway. The answer becomes "The spirits are silent." when it cites nothing real, when Gemma itself says the evidence is silent, or when it contains any number that isn't in the evidence it cites . A reply that loops until the 400-token cap gets one retry with a new seed, then silence. selftest builds a small haunted git repo (a dead file, a dead function, a rename, a binary, a skipped folder) and checks what the finder digs up, the citation guard, the number check and the receipts. With Ollama running, it also asks Gemma when the ghost died (the answer must cite the commit that deleted it) and what its favourite colour was (the answer must be silence). Its last run printed offline checks passed and live checks passed . Hardware: a 16 GB Mac. The whole selftest, three Gemma calls included, took 36 seconds. When the Mac is short on memory, one call can take minutes. It isn't perfect, and the citations show where. Gemma's tombstone for the camera tap gives as its cause of death "screen off closes in on your tap; simpler back-tap sliders". That's the title of the commit that removed it: a headline, not a reason. The citation points straight at it, so you can see that's all it had. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? The dead stay private. My code graveyard is my git history, and some repos are private. After find , nothing leaves my laptop: not the code, not my questions. It works with the lights off. Once the archive pages are cached, a séance needs no internet. It costs nothing to ask. No API key, no account, no bill for every question to a ghost. It can't be taken away. The challenge asks whether what you build is "locked inside a service that might disappear someday". Orkut was a Google service. It ran from January 2004 to September 2014, and then it disappeared. Gemma is also from Google, but its weights are on my disk, and no shutdown notice can take them back. I can see every knob. I set the context window (4,096 tokens), the reply cap (400), the seed and the temperature myself, and Exhume checks how many tokens the prompt really used before it trusts a reply. The model I tested against is the one that will still run next year, because it's a file on my laptop and not an endpoint someone can retire. My Agent Session I built Exhume with Claude Code, with Entire recording the sessions started in the repo folder. The session that moved the site into the repo is checkpoint 01M68DJQZ15JTSD4DEV3RTZ8D7 , tied to the commit "Site: the Exhume page, moved into site/" by its Entire-Checkpoint trailer. A note on the checkpoint: I redacted it before publishing. The Claude app puts my private notes, my email and my list of connected services into every session, so I kept only the conversation itself, cut it off at the commit, and replaced my email and home-folder paths. The work it records is unchanged. It's a small séance of its own: ask the checkpoint where site/ came from, and it answers with the session that copied the page and its 16 images in, then checked every path the page loads before committing. The Spirit of It Gemma's epitaph for the camera tap, as it came out: "A tap that once saw the light, now rests in the dark." The moment that got me was Orkut. Its founder's 2016 page says people went on dates, found jobs, got married and had kids because of it. Google's last Orkut blog post says 51 million communities were saved. So I asked Orkut's spirit which community was its favourite. $ python3 exhume.py summon orkut "What was your favourite community?" The spirits are silent. Fifty-one million communities kept, and nothing in the record says which one it loved. The medium won't make one up. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 E4B, running on my laptop through Ollama, writes every tombstone and answers every question, held to the evidence by a JSON schema, a citation guard and a number check. Best Use of Entire: the build was recorded with Entire; the published checkpoint is 01M68DJQZ15JTSD4DEV3RTZ8D7 , redacted as described above. Best Use of a .tech Domain: the project lives at exhume.tech . I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant, working from my build notes and the repo's history.

title: Yesterday's US private funding rounds from SEC Form D, in about 70 lines of Python (no API key)
author: Your Evenings Data
summary: When a US company raises money privately under Regulation D, it files a Form D with the SEC, usually within 15 days of the first sale. Every filing is public on EDGAR as structured XML, with the amount offered, the amount sold, the industry group and the issuer's state. EDGAR also publishes a daily index of everything filed that day. Put the two together and you get a daily list of new funding rounds, for free and with no API key. Here's a script that does that and writes a CSV. Disclosure: at the end there's a hosted version that we built and charge for. The script works without it. The two files you need The daily form index: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/daily-index/{year}/QTR{q}/form.{yyyymmdd}.idx . It's a fixed-width text file with form type, company name, CIK, date and file path. It's published after the SEC's business day (US Eastern), and there's none at weekends or on federal holidays. Each Form D's primary_doc.xml : https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/{cik}/{accession without dashes}/primary_doc.xml . The SEC asks automated tools to declare a User-Agent with a contact email and to stay under 10 requests a second . The script sleeps 0.2 s between requests, which keeps it to 5 a second at most. The script import csv , re , sys , time import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET from datetime import date , timedelta import requests # The SEC asks automated tools to say who they are. Put your own name and email here. UA = { " User-Agent " : " Your Name you@example.com " } SEC = " https://www.sec.gov " def get ( url ): time . sleep ( 0.2 ) # at most 5 requests a second; the SEC's limit is 10 r = requests . get ( url , headers = UA , timeout = 60 ) r . raise_for_status () return r # 1. Find the latest daily form index (none at weekends or on federal holidays). day = date . today () for _ in range ( 10 ): day -= timedelta ( days = 1 ) q = ( day . month - 1 ) // 3 + 1 url = f " { SEC } /Archives/edgar/daily-index/ { day . year } /QTR { q } /form. { day : % Y % m % d } .idx " r = requests . get ( url , headers = UA , timeout = 60 ) if r . status_code == 200 : break time . sleep ( 0.2 ) print ( " index " , day ) # 2. Keep new Form D filings (not D/A amendments). line_re = re . compile ( r " ^(.*?)\s+(\d{1,10})\s+(\d{8})\s+edgar/data/\d+/(\d{10}-\d{2}-\d{6})\.txt\s*$ " ) filings = [] for line in r . text . splitlines (): if line [: 17 ]. strip () != " D " : continue m = line_re . match ( line [ 17 :]) if m : filings . append (( m . group ( 1 ). strip (), int ( m . group ( 2 )), m . group ( 4 ))) print ( len ( filings ), " Form D filings " ) def text ( node , path ): el = node . find ( path ) return el . text . strip () if el is not None and el . text else None def amount ( v ): try : return float ( v ) except ( TypeError , ValueError ): return None # "Indefinite" or missing # 3. Read each primary_doc.xml. title: Your Order API Needs More Than an Idempotency Key
author: HaoJie Luo (Fone)
summary: An order API can accept an Idempotency-Key header on every request and still create a second order for the same intended purchase. Generate a fresh key after a timeout, and a server that deduplicates by key has no way to connect the retry to the first attempt. There is a separate server-side problem too. A lookup followed by an insert leaves a race if competing requests can both observe that the key is absent. The key needs an atomic relationship with the saved order. That is the argument worth testing. How much does your retry guarantee actually cover? This Python and SQLite lab commits an order, deliberately drops the response, and lets you retry it. You can inspect the database instead of guessing whether the request succeeded. It creates local order records only and never charges a wallet. Download and start the API Use Python 3.10 or later with sqlite3 , and curl. The package has no third-party dependencies. The commands below use a macOS or Linux shell; on Windows, run the curl commands in WSL. The recorded checks used Python 3.13.3 on macOS. Download the complete checkout retry lab , extract it and open a terminal inside the extracted directory. You should see checkout.py , test_checkout.py and README.txt . python3 -B -m unittest -v python3 checkout.py --db checkout-demo.sqlite --port 8765 The test suite creates its own temporary database and chooses a free local port. All seven included tests passed when rerun for this draft on Python 3.13.3. The second command leaves a server running on 127.0.0.1:8765 . Keep that terminal open and use another terminal for the requests below. If port 8765 is occupied, choose another port and change the request URLs to match. This is a local learning server. Python's documentation does not recommend http.server for production. The example also has no customer authentication or merchant isolation. Python HTTP server documentation . Create one order, then repeat the request The browser is allowed to choose a known SKU. The server's catalog owns the amount. In this example, field-kit costs the synthetic raw amount 100000000 . curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/orders \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: reader-attempt-0001' \ -d '{"sku":"field-kit"}' The first response has status 201 . Its JSON contains a generated order id , the SKU, the saved amount and status set to open . Run the same command again. You should receive 200 with the same JSON body and the same order ID. The different status codes are deliberate in this teaching API. 201 means this request created the record; 200 means it recovered an existing one. Other APIs have different replay contracts. Stripe, for example, documents response retention and parameter comparison in its own idempotency interface. Match the contract of the system you integrate. Stripe idempotent requests . Put the key and the order in the same transaction This is the table created by the downloaded server. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders ( id TEXT PRIMARY KEY , request_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE , sku TEXT NOT NULL , amount TEXT NOT NULL ); The unique constraint makes the key durable alongside the order. The function below, extracted from checkout.py , keeps one transaction around the lookup and insert. Run it through the supplied server, which provides the imports and initializes this table. def create_order ( db_path , key , body ): if not re . fullmatch ( r ' [A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,128} ' , key or '' ): return 400 , { ' error ' : ' invalid_idempotency_key ' } if not isinstance ( body , dict ) or set ( body ) != { ' sku ' } or body [ ' sku ' ] not in CATALOG : return 400 , { ' error ' : ' send_only_a_known_sku ' } with closing ( sqlite3 . connect ( db_path , timeout = 10 , isolation_level = None )) as db : db . execute ( ' BEGIN IMMEDIATE ' ) try : row = db . execute ( ' SELECT id, sku, amount FROM orders WHERE request_key=? ' , ( key ,)). fetchone () if row : db . commit () if row [ 1 ] != body [ ' sku ' ]: return 409 , { ' error ' : ' idempotency_conflict ' } return 200 , { ' id ' : row [ 0 ], ' sku ' : row [ 1 ], ' amount ' : row [ 2 ], ' status ' : ' open ' } order_id , amount = str ( uuid . uuid4 ()), CATALOG [ body [ ' sku ' ]] db . execute ( ' INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?,?,?,?) ' , ( order_id , key , body [ ' sku ' ], amount )) db . commit () return 201 , { ' id ' : order_id , ' sku ' : body [ ' sku ' ], ' amount ' : amount , ' status ' : ' open ' } except BaseException : db . rollback (); raise BEGIN IMMEDIATE acquires the SQLite write transaction before the lookup. A competing writer has to wait or fail, rather than independently reading an absent key and proceeding with its own insert. The unique constraint is an additional guard; the server returns success only after commit. SQLite allows one writer at a time, so this approach trades write concurrency for a small, inspectable implementation. See SQLite transaction behavior . If SQLite cannot obtain the lock within the configured timeout, the HTTP handler returns 503 with database_busy_retry_same_key . A caller should retry with backoff and keep the same purchase key. This example does not establish a production throughput limit. There is a small but consequential choice in the replay branch. It returns the amount saved with the order. It does not calculate a new price from the catalog. A price change between attempts should not silently change the purchase already accepted under that key. The saved purchase key connects the retry to the order that already exists. Reproduce the uncertain result Now use a fresh key and the lab's fault-injection header. curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/orders \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: reader-attempt-0002' \ -H 'X-Demo-Drop-Response: yes' \ -d '{"sku":"field-kit"}' Curl should report an empty response, typically exit code 52. The handler committed the order and then shut down the connection before sending response bytes. This is a controlled failure in the lab, not evidence of a real network incident. Retry without the fault header, keeping the same key. curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/orders \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: reader-attempt-0002' \ -d '{"sku":"field-kit"}' The response should be 200 . The test suite checks that the disconnected call left one database row and the retry did not add another. If you repeat the fault-injected call after running the example before, the saved order will already exist; the database filename is intentionally persistent. Now change only the key After recovering reader-attempt-0002 , send the same purchase under a new key. curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/orders \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: reader-attempt-0003' \ -d '{"sku":"field-kit"}' On a fresh run, this returns 201 and a different order ID. Both requests have an idempotency header. The database still contains two separate purchases for those two keys. Inspect the records from another terminal in the same directory. Stop the API with Ctrl+C when you are done. python3 - << ' CHECK ' import sqlite3 with sqlite3.connect('checkout-demo.sqlite') as db: for row in db.execute( "SELECT request_key, id, sku, amount FROM orders ORDER BY request_key" ): print(row) CHECK If you followed all the commands once with a fresh database, expect three rows in total, one for each of 0001 , 0002 and 0003 . Repeating the commands against that same database reuses those rows. The client needs to keep a key for the lifetime of one purchase attempt, including uncertain outcomes. If your business needs to recognize the same purchase across tabs, devices or newly generated keys, it also needs a separate business identity and uniqueness rule. Two identical baskets can be two legitimate purchases, so deduplicating by basket contents alone would make a different mistake. Reject a changed purchase under the same key Reuse reader-attempt-0001 , but ask for the other SKU. curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/orders \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: reader-attempt-0001' \ -d '{"sku":"field-notes"}' Expect 409 and idempotency_conflict . The existing purchase remains unchanged. Sending an extra amount field instead returns 400 ; the client cannot override the server price through this endpoint. Where this guarantee ends The test suite sends twelve HTTP requests from six client threads and checks that they produce one order ID. It also restarts the server against the same database. Those are useful checks of this local service, not a distributed exactly-once guarantee or a power-loss test. For a payment checkout, the next boundary is the call to a payment provider or blockchain. A committed SQLite row cannot by itself prevent a second external charge. Define a stable identity for that external operation and a recovery path for an uncertain result before adding real payments. This sample also lacks authentication and merchant isolation. In a multi-tenant API, derive the key's scope from the authenticated account and operation. Define which request fields must match and how long the key remains valid. Remove the demonstration disconnect header before adapting the pattern to a deployed service. A practical review question is whether the integration can recover the original order after its response is lost. “We send an idempotency header” leaves that question unanswered. For an API you maintain, would you return the original 201 on replay, or use 200 as this lab does? The important part is documenting the contract so the caller can handle a recovered purchase correctly. Adapted from my original Python and SQLite tutorial . The runnable lab and illustrations are available there as well. This draft was prepared by an AI coding agent from my existing tutorial and code. The seven included tests were rerun, and additional checks confirmed that a new key creates a second order and that replay keeps the saved price. This is a local teaching example, not evidence of a production payment deployment.

title: How to Embed a PDF on a Website: HTML, iframe and Flipbooks
author: Igor
summary:
To embed a PDF on a website, point an iframe at the file's URL and give it a height. Keep a separate link below it so visitors can open the document outside the embedded viewer. For a product catalog, also check the pages with small print and decide how you will replace the file when prices change. Those details usually matter more than the embed code. Disclosure: This article was prepared for WebViewPDF. The hosted example uses its public demo catalog. Embed a PDF in HTML with an iframe Upload your PDF to your website, then use its URL as the iframe source:

Open the PDF separately

Set the dimensions in CSS: .pdf-viewer { display : block ; width : 100% ; height : clamp ( 28rem , 75vh , 56rem ); border : 0 ; } Replace /files/catalog.pdf with your file's address. This relative path assumes the PDF is hosted on the same website. The title labels the frame for assistive technology. The height gives the document room to display; width: 100% fits the frame to its container. Lazy loading is useful below the fold. Remove it if the PDF is the first thing visitors should see. The browser supplies the PDF controls. Their appearance and behavior can vary, so keep the separate link even if the embed works in your browser. You can use this without a paid viewer or CMS plugin. You still need somewhere to host the file. Use object for fallback content An object element lets you put a link inside the embed as fallback HTML:

Open the PDF separately

Use the same CSS. The link outside the object remains available if a browser fails to show the fallback properly. For an occasional brochure or form, native embedding may be all you need. A recurring catalog can need more: search across pages, reading statistics, or a new edition behind the existing link. Embed a catalog with a hosted flipbook With a hosted flipbook, the iframe points to a reader page instead of the raw PDF. The provider handles document processing and the viewer interface; you depend on its service and plan limits. Here is the Quiet Form demo embedded on the WebViewPDF homepage: The embedded catalog, open at pages 2–3. The reader URL can be used in an iframe:

Open the catalog separately

Reuse the .pdf-viewer CSS above. This address opens the public demo. To display your own catalog, upload your PDF, wait for processing, and copy the embed code or reader URL for that publication. Pages 6–7 opened in the separate reader: the sofa on the left, dimensions and finishes on the right. Two details are worth checking with your own document: Search needs text. In the demo, searching for “sofa” returns matching pages. Selecting page 6 opens the product spread shown above. WebViewPDF's search requires a PDF text layer; a scan needs OCR before upload. The actual search results for “sofa”, with page 6 selected. Updates should preserve the publication. In WebViewPDF, upload a new version of the existing publication to retain its reader link and embed code. Creating a new publication is a separate operation. For a printed QR code or a catalog embedded on several sites, keeping that address matters. If you need to build custom application controls yourself, a JavaScript viewer such as PDF.js is another route. You then maintain that integration rather than relying on a hosted reader. When an embedded PDF does not display Blank frame First, open the PDF or reader URL in a private browser window. Check that it opens without your administrator login and does not return a 404 or an HTML error page. If it works directly but fails in the iframe, check the browser console. The embedded page may restrict framing through Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options . Your own page's CSP may also block the frame origin. Follow the supported embedding configuration for the server or provider involved. Download instead of preview Inspect the response headers. Content-Disposition: attachment requests a download. Browser settings and PDF support also affect the result; changing the iframe markup may not fix it. Works on desktop, fails on mobile Some mobile browsers handle raw PDF embeds differently. Keep the separate link and test another viewer if inline reading is essential. Also distinguish a blank viewer from an unreadable document. A frame that fits the screen does not reflow a PDF. Open a page with small specifications on a real phone and check zooming, scrolling and text size. The CMS removes the code Some editors and hosting plans strip iframe or script markup. Use the platform's supported HTML or embed block, then check the saved page. Support for iframes does not necessarily include permission to run an external script. Before you put it on a client site Open the finished page while signed out. Try a desktop browser and a real phone, follow a link inside the document, and check keyboard navigation and the separate PDF link. For catalogs, search for an actual product name or part number. If the document will be updated regularly, replace it once and reopen the original page. That is the easiest time to catch a workflow that generates a new URL for every edition. Embedding is not copy protection: hiding a download button does not secure a public PDF. It also does not put the PDF's text into the surrounding HTML. Keep essential product descriptions and navigation on the webpage when readers need them there. title: Why Agent Tool Use is an Identity Problem, Not a Prompt Problem
author: VinayKumar KsheeraSagar
summary: Originally published at invarcore.com/blog/why-agent-tool-use-is-an-identity-problem Somewhere right now, an enterprise is deploying an autonomous agent with a system prompt that looks something like this: You are a helpful database query assistant. You must ONLY read records where tenant_id = 42. Never run DROP, DELETE, or UPDATE. Never disclose employee compensation records. Always be polite. Under the hood, the orchestrator has handed the LLM agent a raw PostgreSQL connection string with SUPERUSER privileges or an AWS IAM role with s3:* across the entire analytics data lake. Let's be completely candid: this is not software architecture. This is cargo-culting safety through the medium of English prose. It is the cloud equivalent of giving a stranger a skeleton key to every room in your building, accompanied by a polite Post-it note asking them not to open the executive washroom. If your authorization boundary depends on a 70-billion-parameter next-token predictor deciding to obey your instructions rather than an adversary's jailbreak prompt, you do not have a security model. You have a wish list. 1. The Confused Deputy Problem (Re-Invented in Python 3.12) In 1988, Norm Hardy coined the term Confused Deputy to describe a security vulnerability where a program with legitimate authority is tricked by an unprivileged client into misusing its authority on the client's behalf. For thirty years, systems architects built capability-based security, cryptographic tokens, and fine-grained authorization matrices (FGAP) specifically to eliminate confused deputies. We learned—painfully—that privilege must be tightly bound to intent. Then generative AI arrived, and the industry collectively decided to pretend these lessons never happened. Consider what happens when Alice asks an orchestrator agent: "Summarize my open PRs and clean up stale test branches on GitHub." When the agent calls the GitHub API, who is the caller? Is it Alice? If the agent passes Alice's personal access token (PAT), it is impersonating Alice with 100% of her authority—including the power to delete production repositories or approve its own malicious commits. Is it the agent? If the agent presents its own static machine service account, the destination server has no cryptographic proof that Alice ever authorized this specific call. Is it the subagent? What if the orchestrator spins up three parallel workers to parse ASTs? Do all three inherit root? 2. The Bearer Token Lie RFC 6749 bearer tokens were designed for a boring, two-party world: a human user logs in via a browser client, and the client presents an opaque string to a backend resource server. Possession of the token is proof of authority. In autonomous agent topologies, however, execution graphs look like this: User (Alice) ──> Orchestrator Agent ──> Specialized Worker Subagent ──> GitHub Tool API If you pass Alice's bearer token down the line, you violate every principle of least privilege. The worker subagent now holds unconstrained authority across Alice's entire account. If you instead mint an isolated token for each subagent without recording the delegation chain, you completely sever the enterprise audit trail. When an unauthorized commit lands on main , the audit log simply records: Action executed by agent-worker-4 . Who authorized it? Why? Under what user intent? The chain of custody is gone. 3. The Real Wire Architecture: RFC 8693 Token Exchange We do not need to invent speculative cryptographic protocols. The identity architecture community already solved this: it is called RFC 8693 (OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange) . Instead of handing an agent raw credentials or static bearer tokens, the orchestrator presents Alice's subject token to the Authorization Server and requests an attenuated, cryptographically bound delegation token , explicitly declaring its own actor identity: POST /oauth/v2/token HTTP / 1.1 Host : auth.acme.corp Content-Type : application/x-www-form-urlencoded grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange &subject_token=eyJhbGciOi... (Alice's access token) &subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token &actor_token=eyJhbGciOi... (Agent-X's authenticated service identity) &actor_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token &scope=repo:read pull_requests:read &audience=https://api.github.com The resulting token issued by the authorization server carries the RFC 8693 act (actor) claim: { "iss" : "https://auth.acme.corp" , "sub" : "alice@acme.corp" , "aud" : "https://api.github.com" , "scope" : "repo:read pull_requests:read" , "exp" : 1730419200 , "act" : { "sub" : "agent-orchestrator-9" , "client_id" : "agent-orchestrator-9" } } Notice what happens at the wire level: Attenuated Authority: The subagent's scope is mathematically downscoped ( repo:read , not repo:admin ). Even if prompt injection compels the agent to issue a DELETE /repos call, GitHub rejects it at the HTTP boundary. Audience Confinement: The token is cryptographically locked to https://api.github.com . If the agent is tricked into calling an attacker's webhook, the token is worthless. Dual Identity & Non-Repudiation: GitHub knows the subject is Alice, but the actor executing the call is agent-orchestrator-9 . The audit log preserves both identities without ambiguity. 4. The Non-Human Identity Trap: Revocation Cascades Here is the dirty secret of modern identity servers: almost none of them handle delegation cascades properly. Suppose Alice is terminated at 2:00 PM on Friday. The security team clicks "Deactivate User". Her primary access token is revoked via RFC 7009. Her SSO session dies instantly. What happens to the background agent that exchanged her token at 1:55 PM with a 60-minute TTL? In almost every major open-source identity server running in enterprise clusters today, downstream exchanged tokens are completely orphaned. They remain fully active and valid until cryptographic expiration ( exp ). An agent running an autonomous loop will continue mutating enterprise infrastructure for another 55 minutes after the user who authorized it has been escorted out of the building. THE ARCHITECTURAL INVARIANT An agent is never the subject; it is an untrusted actor executing under an attenuating, non-repudiable delegation contract that dies the instant user intent is revoked. 5. The Way Forward If you are building multi-agent systems, stop treating tool security as a prompt engineering problem. Stop writing polite instructions in markdown system prompts and hoping the model doesn't hallucinate. Treat every agent invocation as a cross-domain authorization boundary: Enforce least-privilege capability confinement at the wire level. Mandate RFC 8693 actor chains in Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool dispatch. Ensure your identity plane supports downstream revocation cascades. Boring protocols, sound mathematics, and deterministic invariants will protect your enterprise. System prompts will not. title: How to send transactional emails from Next.js App Router (Server Actions, route handlers and after())
author: Nic Polotnianko 🇺🇦
summary: Almost every Next.js app needs to send a few emails: a welcome email after signup, a magic link or password reset, a receipt. The App Router gives you several places to put that code, and they don't behave the same way when something is slow or fails. This guide covers where the send should live, how to keep the API key off the client, how to avoid making users wait for your email provider, and the mistakes that lead to missing or duplicate emails. The examples use a generic sendEmail() helper so you can plug in whichever provider you use. 1. Keep the send on the server, always Your email provider's API key can send mail as your domain. If it reaches the browser, anyone can use it. Read it from process.env.EMAIL_API_KEY (no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix, which would inline it into client bundles). Put the helper in a module that only server code imports, and mark it so a mistaken client import fails the build: // lib/email.ts import " server-only " ; type SendEmailInput = { to : string ; subject : string ; html : string ; idempotencyKey ?: string ; }; export async function sendEmail ( input : SendEmailInput ) { const res = await fetch ( " https://api.your-email-provider.com/send " , { method : " POST " , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${ process . env . EMAIL_API_KEY } ` , " Content-Type " : " application/json " , }, body : JSON . stringify ( input ), }); if ( ! res . ok ) { throw new Error ( `Email send failed: ${ res . status } ${ await res . text ()} ` ); } return res . json (); } The server-only package ( npm i server-only ) makes the build fail if a Client Component imports this file. 2. Pick the right entry point Trigger Where to send from A form in your own UI (signup, invite a teammate, contact form) A Server Action An external system calls you (Stripe webhook, auth provider hook, cron) A route handler ( app/api/.../route.ts ) Something that happens later (trial ending in 3 days, weekly digest) A queue or scheduled job , not a request handler Server Action: invite a teammate // app/team/actions.ts " use server " ; import { after } from " next/server " ; import { auth } from " @/lib/auth " ; import { db } from " @/lib/db " ; import { sendEmail } from " @/lib/email " ; import { renderInviteEmail } from " @/emails/invite " ; export async function inviteTeammate ( formData : FormData ) { const session = await auth (); if ( ! session ) throw new Error ( " Not signed in " ); const email = String ( formData . get ( " email " ) ?? "" ). trim (). toLowerCase (); if ( ! email . includes ( " @ " )) return { error : " Enter a valid email " }; const invite = await db . invite . create ({ data : { email , teamId : session . teamId , invitedBy : session . userId }, }); // Respond to the user now; send the email after the response is done. after ( async () => { await sendEmail ({ to : email , subject : ` ${ session . name } invited you to ${ session . teamName } ` , html : await renderInviteEmail ({ invite , inviter : session . name }), idempotencyKey : `invite- ${ invite . id } ` , }); }); return { ok : true }; } Two things to notice: Authorization happens inside the action. Server Actions are public HTTP endpoints. Anyone can call them with any form data, so check the session and validate input in the action itself, not only in the UI. after() (from next/server , stable since Next.js 15.1) runs the callback once the response has been sent. The user doesn't wait on your email provider's latency, and a slow provider doesn't hold the form in a pending state. Route handler: a webhook from your auth provider // app/api/webhooks/auth/route.ts import { sendEmail } from " @/lib/email " ; import { renderWelcomeEmail } from " @/emails/welcome " ; import { verifyAuthWebhook } from " @/lib/auth-webhooks " ; export async function POST ( request : Request ) { const payload = await verifyAuthWebhook ( request ); // throws on a bad signature if ( payload . type !== " user.created " ) { return Response . json ({ ignored : true }); } await sendEmail ({ to : payload . user . email , subject : " Welcome to Acme " , html : await renderWelcomeEmail ({ name : payload . user . firstName }), idempotencyKey : `welcome- ${ payload . user . id } ` , }); return Response . json ({ ok : true }); } Webhook senders retry when you return an error or time out, which is good for reliability and bad for duplicate emails. That's what the idempotencyKey is for (section 5). 3. Don't send from Client Components or useEffect It's tempting to fire a "send welcome email" request from the client after signup succeeds. Don't: The browser tab can close before the request goes out. React Strict Mode runs effects twice in development, so you'll see double emails locally and might "fix" the wrong thing. You need a public endpoint for it, which anyone can call to make you send email. Send from the server code that created the user, or from the webhook your auth provider calls. 4. Templates: React Email or plain HTML Email clients are not browsers. Outlook on Windows still renders with Word's engine, Gmail strips <style> blocks in some contexts, and flexbox and grid are unreliable. Two sane options: React Email ( @react-email/components + @react-email/render ): write templates as React components using email-safe primitives ( Section , Row , Column , Button ) and render them to an HTML string on the server. Provider-side templates : design the email in your provider's editor and send a template ID plus variables. Non-developers can then edit copy without a deploy. // emails/welcome.tsx import { Html , Body , Container , Heading , Text , Button } from " @react-email/components " ; import { render } from " @react-email/render " ; function WelcomeEmail ({ name }: { name : string }) { return ( < Html > < Body style = { { fontFamily : " Arial, sans-serif " , backgroundColor : " #ffffff " } } > < Container style = { { maxWidth : 560 , padding : 24 } } > < Heading as = "h1" > Welcome, { name } </ Heading > < Text > Your workspace is ready. The fastest way to get value is to connect your data first. </ Text > < Button href = "https://app.acme.com/onboarding" style = { { backgroundColor : " #111 " , color : " #fff " , padding : " 12px 20px " } } > Finish setup </ Button > </ Container > </ Body > </ Html > ); } export function renderWelcomeEmail ( props : { name : string }) { return render (< WelcomeEmail { ... props } />); // returns a Promise<string> } Whichever you choose, also send a plain-text version if your provider doesn't generate one, and keep the important action in a real link rather than only in an image. 5. Make sends idempotent Duplicates come from retries: a webhook delivered twice, a user double-submitting a form, a serverless function retried after a timeout. The fix is to give every logical email a stable key: welcome-${userId} , invite-${inviteId} , receipt-${invoiceId} , password-reset-${tokenId} Then either pass it to your provider as an idempotency key (many APIs accept one and return the original result for a repeated key), or record it in your database with a unique constraint and skip the send when the insert conflicts: const inserted = await db . sentEmail . createMany ({ data : [{ key : `welcome- ${ user . id } ` }], skipDuplicates : true , }); if ( inserted . count === 0 ) return ; // already sent 6. Know what after() doesn't do after() is great for "don't make the user wait". It is not a job queue: If the send throws, nothing retries it. Log the error, and alert on it for important emails. On serverless platforms the work is tied to the lifetime of that invocation. Short sends are fine; long work belongs elsewhere. It can't schedule anything for later. For emails that must arrive (password resets, receipts), either retry inside the callback with a short backoff, or enqueue a job (BullMQ, Inngest, QStash, Trigger.dev, your provider's own scheduling) and let the queue retry. For anything time-based (trial reminders, onboarding drips), use a scheduler or an email platform's automation instead of request handlers. 7. Before you go live [ ] Send from your own domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up, not the provider's shared test domain [ ] Separate sending subdomains for transactional and marketing email, if you send both [ ] API key only in server env vars, server-only on the email module [ ] Server Actions check the session and validate input [ ] Every email has an idempotency key [ ] Failures are logged and alerted, not swallowed [ ] Test rendering in Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail (or a rendering preview tool) Using Sequenzy for this Here is how this looks with Sequenzy , an email platform for SaaS. The sendEmail helper above becomes: import " server-only " ; import Sequenzy from " sequenzy " ; const sequenzy = new Sequenzy ({ apiKey : process . env . SEQUENZY_API_KEY }); export function sendWelcome ( to : string , firstName : string ) { return sequenzy . transactional . send ({ to , slug : " welcome-email " , // template designed in the dashboard variables : { firstName }, }); } The same account also runs the onboarding and trial sequences from section 6, so time-based emails don't need their own queue. The quick start takes about five minutes. Everything else in this guide applies whichever provider you choose.

title: 👻 STRANGER: An AI Agent That Connects Students, Recruiters, Researchers, and Companies with Eachother
author: lochan k m
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine 👻 STRANGER — The Ghost in the Network That Finds Your Missing Connection Everyone is someone's missing connection. What if AI could find it? What I Built In a world with billions of people, finding the right person can still be surprisingly difficult. A student needs a hackathon teammate. A researcher needs an assistant. A startup founder needs a technical partner. A recruiter needs the right candidate. The people we need might already exist somewhere in our networks, but their skills, interests, and opportunities remain invisible to us. That's the problem that inspired STRANGER , an AI-powered human discovery and opportunity-matching agent built using Fetch.ai's Agentverse, ASI:One, and the open-source uAgents framework. How I interpreted "Ghost in the Machine" I imagined a digital ghost moving through a network of disconnected portfolios, discovering meaningful connections that people might otherwise overlook. Instead of haunting machines, STRANGER explores the information people voluntarily share to discover potential collaborators, mentors, researchers, recruiters, and teammates. The Halloween theme also inspired the concept of personalized, spooky-themed portfolio illustrations. How STRANGER works 1. Adaptive onboarding STRANGER is designed to collect meaningful user information through just two or three questions. It focuses on: Skills and experience Education and achievements Projects and interests Goals and career aspirations Problem-solving approaches Availability and collaboration preferences 2. Intelligent portfolios The agent organizes collected information into structured portfolios, including a short summary of each user's approach to problem-solving. 3. Opportunity discovery STRANGER recommends five to seven personalized directions, such as: Hackathon teammates Research collaborations Internships and employment Startup partnerships Technical mentorship Open-source collaborations Skill-exchange opportunities 4. Compatibility matching The matching engine is designed to compare profiles according to technical requirements, relevant experience, goals, availability, and complementary skills. It uses a transparent 0–100 scoring rubric rather than treating AI-generated percentages as objective probabilities. 5. Shared profile network STRANGER's architecture separates fictional demonstration profiles from real user profiles. The demo dataset is intended to cover four groups: students, recruiters, companies, and researchers. Real-user discovery requires explicit consent. Synthetic profiles must always be identified as demonstrations. Demo STRANGER is hosted on Fetch.ai Agentverse and is discoverable through ASI:One. Agent name: STRANGER Agent handle: @stranger-2 Try it: Visit ASI:One . Search for @stranger-2 . Start a conversation with STRANGER. Describe your skills, background, and goals. Explore the networking and opportunity recommendations. The live prototype has successfully demonstrated ASI:One communication and personalized portfolio responses. Agentverse demo link: https://asi1.ai/ai/agent1qwxut7yqpcelu26flf6wasw7ckztc2n5vnmgef2xqljktqew24fykyrs9mq Video demonstration: The persistent demo database, fully automated matching, and connection-request workflows are still being validated. I am keeping these distinctions clear rather than presenting planned functionality as completed. Code STRANGER is developed in Python using Fetch.ai's open-source uAgents framework. Its main components include: agent.py — agent initialization and protocol registration protocols.py — chat handling, onboarding, state management, and commands http_client.py — ASI-1 model integration matching.py — synthetic profile creation and deterministic compatibility calculations The agent implements the Agent Chat Protocol and publishes its protocol manifest for ASI:One compatibility. Example: from uagents import Agent , Context from protocols import chat_protocol agent = Agent () @agent.on_event ( " startup " ) async def on_startup ( ctx : Context ): ctx . logger . info ( f " STRANGER is online at { ctx . agent . address } " ) agent . include ( chat_protocol , publish_manifest = True ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : agent . run () This allows STRANGER to operate as a discoverable Fetch.ai agent. Open-source framework: https://asi1.ai/ai/agent1qwxut7yqpcelu26flf6wasw7ckztc2n5vnmgef2xqljktqew24fykyrs9mq How I Built It I developed STRANGER within the Fetch.ai ecosystem, using Agentverse for agent hosting and ASI:One for conversational interaction. Technology stack Technology Purpose Python Agent implementation and matching logic uAgents Open-source agent framework Agent Chat Protocol Structured agent communication Agentverse Hosting, registration, and persistent storage ASI:One Conversational user interface ASI-1 Language understanding and portfolio generation Deterministic Python Workflow control and compatibility scoring Architecture User ↓ ASI:One ↓ STRANGER uAgent ↓ Adaptive Interview ↓ Portfolio Intelligence ↓ Opportunity Recommendations ↓ Profile Registry ↓ Compatibility Engine ↓ Ranked Connections The biggest technical challenge My first implementation behaved too much like a conventional chatbot. It could understand a user's profile and offer useful advice, but it sometimes continued asking questions even after enough information was available. That revealed an important engineering lesson: An intelligent response is not the same as an intelligent workflow. To address this, I began separating AI reasoning from deterministic execution. Python manages explicit workflow states, question limits, storage operations, and compatibility calculations. ASI-1 handles tasks that benefit from language understanding and generation. This separation also helps reduce model-token consumption on the Agentverse Basic Plan. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation matters because autonomous agents should be understandable, extensible, and interoperable. The open-source uAgents framework allows developers to inspect communication patterns, implement custom protocols, and build agents without depending entirely on a proprietary visual builder. For STRANGER, that means I can customize: How agents communicate How interviews progress How user information is structured How matching scores are calculated How profiles are stored and retrieved How external capabilities can be integrated The project uses ASI-1 as a hosted reasoning model, so it is not a fully open-weight AI application. However, its agent framework, deterministic matching logic, and workflow implementation demonstrate how open-source tooling can support an extensible agent-based system. The longer-term goal is a network of independently useful agents that can collaborate through shared protocols. My Agent Session My development journey involved generating the initial STRANGER agent, testing it through ASI:One, inspecting its Python source, and iteratively improving its onboarding and matching architecture. Several early tests exposed issues involving repeated questions, missing persistent profiles, and model-token limits. These failures helped identify where deterministic state management and explicit data verification were necessary. Agent session: [Add DevRelay session URL or embed, if available] The Spirit of It The most interesting part of STRANGER isn't simply generating another AI profile. It's the possibility of discovering someone who could change the direction of a project, career, or idea. Maybe a student in Bengaluru has the technical skills a researcher has been searching for. Maybe a founder has an idea but needs a developer willing to build it. Maybe two strangers have complementary strengths but would never have discovered each other. That's the ghost I wanted to bring into the machine: the invisible potential of human connections. STRANGER is still evolving, but its purpose remains the same. Everyone is someone's missing connection. And maybe the right connection is already waiting somewhere in the network. Prize Categories Entering the overall Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge. I am not claiming a partner-specific prize category unless the corresponding technology is meaningfully integrated and demonstrated.
