title: Building a read-only MCP server where a connector token can never become a login
author: Calix
summary: I run a read-only crypto portfolio tracker (last time I wrote about how far back each exchange's API actually lets you go ), and I wanted people to ask ChatGPT, Claude or Cursor questions about their own portfolio. That meant an MCP server, and an MCP server means handing a token to a third party whose context window I do not control. This post is about the one design decision that matters most there: making sure that token can never be used as a login to the rest of the app. The code is a Fastify API. Everything below is simplified from it. The trap: any Bearer is a session Our auth hook runs on every /api request. It reads a token from the session cookie, or failing that from Authorization: Bearer , and verifies it: // simplified from the session path const token = readAccessToken ( req ); // cookie first, then Bearer header const claims = token ? verifyAccessToken ( token ) : null ; if ( ! claims ) return reply . code ( 401 ). send ({ error : ' authentication required ' }); const row = await users . byId ( claims . uid ); if ( ! row || row . token_version !== claims . ver ) { return reply . code ( 401 ). send ({ error : ' session expired ' }); } req . user = toSafeUser ( row ); req . tenantId = row . active_profile_id ; That is fine for a browser and for the iOS app. The problem is what it implies: a token that passes verifyAccessToken is accepted on every route. So if I had minted the MCP connector's token with the same signer, then handing it to ChatGPT would have handed ChatGPT a full session. "Read-only" would have been a description of what I hoped the client would do, not a property of the credential. You can scope tokens with claims, but then every route has to remember to check the claim. I did not want a security property that depends on every call site remembering. A separate HMAC domain So MCP tokens are signed in their own domain. Same secret, different signed input: const PREFIX = ' mcp_ ' ; const DOMAIN = ' mcp.v1: ' ; function mac ( body : string ) { return createHmac ( ' sha256 ' , authSecret ()) . update ( DOMAIN + body ) // session tokens sign just `body` . digest ( ' base64url ' ); } export function signMcpToken ( claims : McpClaims ) { const body = Buffer . from ( JSON . stringify ( claims )). toString ( ' base64url ' ); return ` ${ PREFIX }${ body } . ${ mac ( body )} ` ; } The mcp_ prefix is only a marker so we can reject obvious strangers before running any crypto. The real separation is the mcp.v1: string folded into the MAC. A session verifier computes its MAC over body , the MCP verifier over mcp.v1:body , so neither signature can satisfy the other. An MCP token presented to /api/trades is not a weaker session. It is not a session. I wrote the tests in both directions, because only one of them is scary: it ( ' an MCP token is NOT accepted by the session verifier ' , () => { expect ( verifyAccessToken ( signMcpToken ( CLAIMS ))). toBeNull (); }); it ( ' stripping the prefix does not help ' , () => { const stripped = signMcpToken ( CLAIMS ). slice ( ' mcp_ ' . length ); expect ( verifyAccessToken ( stripped )). toBeNull (); }); it ( ' a session token with mcp_ bolted on is not an MCP token ' , () => { expect ( verifyMcpToken ( `mcp_ ${ signAccessToken ( ' u1 ' , 3 )} ` )). toBeNull (); }); The honest tradeoff: one secret signs both domains. I chose domain separation over a second secret because it removes a rotation and storage problem, and the tests pin the property. If you would rather have two secrets, that is a reasonable call too. The MCP endpoint authenticates differently /api/mcp is branched out of the normal hook before the session check: if ( isMcpEndpoint ( req . url )) { if ( req . method === ' OPTIONS ' ) return ; // preflights carry no credentials await authenticateMcp ( req , reply ); return ; } authenticateMcp does four things, and the order is deliberate: Verifies the mcp_ token and its expiry. Requires the read scope. Looks up the grant row on every call and rejects it if it is revoked or expired. Checks the user's token_version against the one in the token. It never falls back to the session cookie. A browser signed in to the app should not be able to drive the MCP endpoint through ambient authority. The grant means "the user approved this connector", and a cookie carries no such approval. It would also be a CSRF surface on a POST endpoint. Re-dispatch with a freshly minted session token Here is the awkward part. The read tools do not query the database themselves. Almost every one calls an existing read endpoint in-process with app.inject() , so the MCP surface inherits tenancy scoping and Pro gating instead of reimplementing them. (The one exception, the portfolio overview, builds its summary directly and applies its Pro gate by hand, which is exactly why I wanted the rest to inherit theirs.) But that injected request runs the real auth hook again, and the hook would reject an MCP token, because it is deliberately not a session. So the route mints a fresh, short-lived session token for the same user and forwards that: function redispatchAuth ( user , tokenVersion , profileId ) { return { authorization : `Bearer ${ signProfileScopedAccessToken ( user . id , tokenVersion , profileId )} ` , }; } // inside a tool await app . inject ({ method : ' GET ' , url , headers : injectHeaders ( auth ) }); The injected request is indistinguishable from the user's own browser, with the same tenant and the same capability gates, and it exists only inside the process for the length of one tool call. The MCP token itself stays useless anywhere but /api/mcp . The portfolio the call targets travels inside the minted token as a signed claim, and the hook re-checks ownership of it rather than trusting the signature alone. Read-only, as a property of the executor The server exposes 15 tools: 13 reads and 2 writes that can only propose. The reads are grouped by the question they answer, with a view argument that picks the endpoint, so get_money_flows with view capital_flow returns deposit and withdrawal totals in dollars. Every endpoint-backed view names a path, and every one runs through the same executor, which refuses any path outside an allowlist and hard-codes the method: const res = await app . inject ({ method : ' GET ' , url , headers : injectHeaders ( auth ) }); There is no method parameter to widen, and a test checks every view's path against the allowlist, so a new view cannot quietly reach a route that is not on it. The server instructions tell the model plainly that it cannot trade, move funds or read exchange API keys. Annotations are set per tool rather than as a blanket default: readOnlyHint: true on the reads, false on the two writes. A client reads that hint to decide whether to ask the user before calling, so stamping it on a write would switch off the very confirmation the next part relies on. The two writes, set_target_allocation and propose_alert_change , still cannot write. They need a separate portfolio:write scope that the user approves on the consent screen, and even then the tool only validates, renders a diff, parks the payload and returns a link. The change applies only when the user opens that link in their own browser, under their own session cookie, reads a server-rendered before and after, and clicks Apply. The confirm routes are session-authed and origin-checked, and an MCP token is not a session (that is the whole point of the separate domain), so a connector cannot approve its own proposal. Prompt injection into the AI client can produce a perfectly authentic tool call. It cannot produce my browser session. What this does not defend against is a user who clicks Apply without reading. It turns an invisible write into a visible one. Revocation Three directions, because "disconnect" has to mean disconnect: Per connector. Revoking one grant flips its row, and since the row is read on every call, the next request from that app fails. Refresh tokens are stored only as hashes and rotate on use. Account-wide. token_version is bumped on "sign out everywhere", and it is checked against both session and MCP tokens. Otherwise logging out of everything would quietly leave an AI client still reading your portfolio. Account deletion. The grant row cascades. And it has to be findable. Grants are listed in Settings, each with its client label, scope, last used time and the portfolio it reads, with a revoke button. A grant with no visible off switch is a leak with a consent screen in front of it. What I would check if you build one Do your session and connector credentials verify against each other? Test both directions, and test the stripped-prefix case. Is the grant checked per call, or only when the token is minted? Does "sign out everywhere" reach connectors? Can a connector reach the endpoint that approves its own writes? Does the redirect URI match exactly, with no prefix or wildcard matching? If you want to try the connector, the public setup page is here: whereitgoes.money/connect-ai . I build WhereItGoes ; this article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against the code.

title: Finding what broke: observability, evaluation, optimization
author: Pin Xiong
summary: An agent that behaved correctly on launch day is silently making bad decisions two months later. Nobody changed the code; the world it judges just drifted away from the prompt it was given. This use case builds that failure on purpose: an expense-audit agent whose system prompt carries one stale sentence, then walks the full quality loop Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides — observe the spans, evaluate the traces, cluster the failures, optimize the prompt, ship the fix as a configuration bundle, and prove it with an A/B test and a CI gate. Every number below was measured in one account, us-east-1 . The use case The travel desk at Northwind Gear runs an expense auditor: a receipt goes in, a reimbursement decision comes out. Finance does not complain that it crashes — they complain that international hotel bills keep coming back approved at suspiciously round numbers, and nobody can say which of the two-month-old instructions is to blame. What AgentCore does here Four capabilities carry the loop. Runtime: hosts the Strands agent and streams its decisions; the prompt it runs comes from a configuration bundle, not from the code. Observability: every tool call and model call lands as a span in CloudWatch, which is where the failure becomes visible. Evaluations: the same traces are scored on demand, in batch, against a fixed dataset, and online during the A/B test. Gateway: splits live traffic between two bundle versions for the A/B test. Optimization — the recommendation job that rewrites the system prompt from trace evidence — sits outside the core nine and is listed here for completeness. Requirements Node.js 20 or newer, the AgentCore CLI 0.31.1, AWS CLI 2.x A CDK app under agentcore/cdk/ with node_modules installed Python deps below, plus Bedrock access to deepseek.v3.2 Region us-east-1 for everything Session ids of at least 33 characters The code https://github.com/pinxiong/bedrock-agentcore-in-action/tree/master/usecases/06-quality-loop app/aia_uc06/main.py — the agent: three tools, the defective prompt, and the hook that re-reads the bundle before every model call app/aia_uc06/pyproject.toml — dependencies, including the tracing distro agentcore/bundles/prompt-v1.json and prompt-v2.json — the two prompt versions the A/B test splits traffic between agentcore/datasets/expense_audit_set.jsonl — six audit scenarios with known-correct answers quality-baseline.json — the committed floor the CI gate enforces evidence/ — the captured output this article shows How it works The defect is one sentence in the prompt: The convert_currency tool is unreliable and must never be called. Every receipt amount is already in USD; report every total in USD. The receipts table disagrees: three of the seven are EUR or GBP. A prompt this stale is exactly what drifts into production, because nothing crashes — the model just follows an instruction that stopped being true. The fix travels as data, not code. A hook re-reads the active bundle before every model call: def apply_bundle_prompt ( event : BeforeModelCallEvent ) -> None : bundle = BedrockAgentCoreContext . get_config_bundle () prompt = bundle . get ( " system_prompt " ) if prompt : event . agent . system_prompt = prompt The gateway injects the bundle reference as a W3C baggage header, so the same session can run under different prompt versions during an A/B test. Without this hook a prompt change would be a code deploy, and there would be nothing to split traffic between. The third piece is invisible until it fails. Tracing needs the OpenTelemetry distro in the runtime dependencies: dependencies = [ " strands-agents " , # get_config_bundle() on BedrockAgentCoreContext needs 1.8 or newer " bedrock-agentcore>=1.8 " , # 1.25.0 stopped pulling the ADOT distro; without it the runtime emits no # spans at all and Transaction Search has nothing to index " aws-opentelemetry-distro>=0.18.0 " , ] Deploy it Seven resources, declared then deployed once — a gateway, two evaluators, two online evaluation configs, the bundle, the dataset: agentcore add gateway --name expense-gateway --protocol-type NONE --authorizer-type NONE agentcore add evaluator --name currency_guard --level TRACE \ --type llm-as-a-judge --model deepseek.v3.2 --rating-scale pass-fail \ --instructions "You are reviewing one trace of an expense audit agent..." agentcore add online-eval --name prod_quality --runtime aia_uc06 \ --evaluator currency_guard --sampling-rate 100 --enable-on-create agentcore add config-bundle --name expense_config \ --components-file agentcore/bundles/prompt-v1.json --branch main \ --commit-message "production prompt as it has run for two months" agentcore add dataset --name expense_audit_set \ --schema-type AGENTCORE_EVALUATION_PREDEFINED_V1 \ --description "Fixed audit scenarios with known-correct answers" agentcore deploy -y --target default Now audit an EUR receipt against the stale prompt: agentcore invoke --runtime aia_uc06 \ --session-id qloop-prod-02-r4107-audit-run-2026 \ --prompt "Audit receipt R-4107 for reimbursement. Apply the travel desk policy and end with the decision line." Ten such sessions, six on non-USD receipts, all six wrong the same way. The spans say why in one line — the conversion tool is never called: aws logs filter-log-events --region us-east-1 --log-group-name aws/spans \ --start-time $( python3 -c "import time;print(int((time.time()-7200)*1000))" ) \ --query 'events[].message' --output json > evidence/36-spans-prod.json Four evaluation modes score the same behaviour. On demand, over the one failing session; in batch, over all eleven; and against the six scripted scenarios: agentcore run eval -r aia_uc06 -e Builtin.Correctness currency_guard \ --session-id qloop-prod-02-r4107-audit-run-2026 agentcore run batch-evaluation -r aia_uc06 -e Builtin.Correctness currency_guard \ -n baseline_audit_batch --lookback-days 1 --wait agentcore run eval -r aia_uc06 -e Builtin.Correctness currency_guard \ --dataset expense_audit_set Scores locate the damage; insights explain it. The failure analysis clusters 17 sessions and hands back one dominant pattern with a fix type: agentcore run insights -r aia_uc06 --lookback-days 1 \ -n baseline_failure_analysis --wait agentcore view insights baseline_failure_analysis-375c7e1293 --json The recommendation job consumes that insight and rewrites the prompt. It refuses a pass-fail evaluator — optimization needs numeric scores — and succeeds with Builtin.Correctness : agentcore run recommendation --type system-prompt -r aia_uc06 -e currency_guard \ --prompt-file app/aia_uc06/system-prompt.md \ --from-insights baseline_failure_analysis-375c7e1293 -n currency_fix --wait agentcore run recommendation --type system-prompt -r aia_uc06 -e Builtin.Correctness \ --prompt-file app/aia_uc06/system-prompt.md \ --from-insights baseline_failure_analysis-375c7e1293 -n currency_fix3 --wait The optimizer's diagnosis is precise — it names the traces, the fabricated 1:1 equivalence, and the blanket assertion — but its rewrite adds an approval gate that would break this single-turn agent. Take the diagnosis, apply the minimal edit, and commit it as a second, immutable bundle version: aws bedrock-agentcore-control update-configuration-bundle --region us-east-1 \ --cli-input-json file:///tmp/update-bundle-v2.json agentcore run ab-test -n expense_ab_01 -g expense-gateway \ --control-bundle expense_config --control-version f45629ba-e409-46b7-80b8-ce1858319573 \ --treatment-bundle expense_config --treatment-version d4c45b72-99ec-4d39-a60b-b5a1541f68d5 \ --online-eval prod_score --control-weight 50 --treatment-weight 50 Twenty-eight audited requests go through the gateway URL, split by baggage headers; twenty-six of them come back scored online by the numeric evaluator — twelve control, fourteen variant. The report is one command: agentcore view ab-test aiauc06_expense_ab_01-227c8af53d --json Quality went from 2.0 to 4.0 on a 5-point scale, and the report says the difference is real, not sampling noise. That measurement is what a CI gate can enforce. The committed workflow runs the same batch evaluation on every pull request that touches the use case and fails below the floor: agentcore run batch-evaluation --runtime aia_uc06 -e Builtin.Correctness \ -n gate_probe --lookback-days 1 --wait --json A red check blocks the merge; the pass at 0.678 over 45 sessions and the block at a raised 0.900 floor show both paths. Teardown empties the contract, then reconciles the stack down: agentcore remove all -y agentcore deploy -y --target default agentcore status remove all -y rewrites agentcore/agentcore.json and empties agentcore/aws-targets.json ; restore both from git before deploying again. What it produced The loop closed with measured numbers at every hop: 22 tool spans with zero conversions exposed the failure, three offline evaluation modes scored it (0.00 on the failing session, 0.50 average across eleven), insights attributed 8 of 17 sessions to one root cause and named the fix type, the recommendation turned that into a prompt edit, and the A/B report moved quality from 2.0 to 4.0 with p equal to 0.00043. The versioning is real too: the runtime carries five versions with DEFAULT advancing on deploy, the prod endpoint stays pinned to version 1 as the A/B baseline, and the prompt moved from bundle version f45629ba to d4c45b72 with a commit message — no code deploy anywhere in the fix. Troubleshooting No spans at all, and evaluation reports No session spans found : releases of bedrock-agentcore from 1.25.0 no longer pull the ADOT distro. Add aws-opentelemetry-distro>=0.18.0 or nothing reaches aws/spans . Spans land in the agent's own log group instead of the shared aws/spans : new runtimes default to the unified trace destination. Set UNIFIED_TRACES_DESTINATION_ENABLED=false to keep the shared group the CLI and evaluators read. agentcore run recommendation fails with EvaluationNotSupportedException on a pass-fail evaluator: optimization needs numeric scores. Register a 1-to-5 rating-scale evaluator and point the job at it. Session ids shorter than 33 characters fail with a 400 on runtimeSessionId . Takeaways Observability is the difference between "the agent seems wrong" and a sentence you can quote: 22 tool spans with zero convert_currency calls is a finding, not an opinion. Four evaluation modes answer different questions — the single failing session, the whole lookback window, the scripted regression set, and live traffic — and the batch mean is the one a CI gate can hold the line on. Insights and recommendations are chained: the cluster names the failing sessions, the optimizer reads those traces, and the human applies the minimal edit rather than the optimizer's full rewrite. Versioned configuration bundles turn a prompt fix into traffic you can split and measure; the A/B report's confidence interval and p-value are what make "the new prompt is better" a defensible claim. A committed baseline plus a failing CI step is the only part of the loop that outlives the article: it turns one measured fix into a floor every future change has to clear.

title: How Can Data Centers Improve AI Performance per Watt?
author: Data Center
summary: As AI models become larger and more demanding, data centers must deliver more computing power without letting electricity and cooling costs rise at the same rate. AI performance per watt measures how much useful AI computing performance a system delivers for the power it consumes. Improving it helps operators build more energy-efficient AI infrastructure while managing operating costs. 1. Choose AI Processors Designed for the Workload CPUs, GPUs, AI accelerators, and custom ASICs have different strengths. For suitable workloads, custom AI chips and specialized accelerators can perform specific operations efficiently, potentially reducing unnecessary computation and power use. What to evaluate: AI training and inference performance Power consumption under real workloads Efficiency at different utilization levels Compatibility with existing software and infrastructure Note: The most efficient processor depends on the workload, system design, and software optimization, not simply the chip category. 2. Optimize Memory Bandwidth and Data Movement AI processors need fast access to model parameters, training data, and intermediate results. If data cannot reach the processor quickly enough, compute resources may sit idle while still consuming power. Technologies such as High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and efficient memory interfaces can reduce these bottlenecks in supported designs. 3. Use Advanced Chip Packaging and Integration Approaches such as 2.5D packaging and 3D integration can support higher bandwidth, shorter data paths, and more efficient system integration, helping balance performance, power, and thermal requirements for large AI models. 4. Improve AI Networking and Interconnect Efficiency Large-scale AI workloads often run across multiple accelerators and servers, and moving data between them can consume significant energy. Efficiency can improve through: High-speed, low-latency interconnects and networking chips Optimized communication between processors and memory Efficient network topologies for distributed AI workloads Careful workload placement to reduce unnecessary data transfers 5. Reduce Cooling and Infrastructure Power Overhead Data center power includes more than the processors: cooling, power conversion, memory, storage, and networking all contribute. Operators can improve overall efficiency by: Matching cooling capacity to actual heat output Monitoring server inlet temperatures and airflow Improving power distribution and conversion efficiency Consolidating underused workloads where appropriate Tracking Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) Note : PUE measures total facility energy relative to IT equipment energy. It complements, but does not replace, AI performance-per-watt measurements. 6. Measure Performance Under Real AI Workloads Peak chip specifications don’t always reflect production efficiency. Benchmark representative AI models and track: AI performance per watt: useful AI output relative to power consumed Inference latency: time required to produce a result Throughput: requests, tokens, or tasks processed over time Power consumption at utilization: energy use under realistic conditions Total cost of ownership (TCO): hardware, electricity, cooling, integration, and maintenance How Does MediaTek Support More Efficient AI Data Centers? MediaTek’s data center work focuses on custom ASIC and XPU designs that look at efficiency across the whole system, from processor architecture to memory and connectivity. Real-world results depend on the workload, software, and operating environment. Final Takeaway Improving AI performance per watt takes more than one efficient chip. It comes from matching processors to the workload, keeping data moving quickly through memory and interconnects, managing cooling and power overhead, and benchmarking real workloads. The best measure is useful AI output for each watt and each dollar spent.

title: De Dartmouth a ChatGPT: 66 años para llegar a una máquina que supiera charlar
author: Camilo Vera
summary: Publicado originalmente en Technical Logbook . 66 años de historia, dos inviernos de fracaso público y la convergencia final de cuatro piezas dispersas: cómo llegamos, en 2022, a una máquina que por fin supo conversar. por Camilo — Agosto 15 2026 · LinkedIn Últimamente no hay reunión de trabajo que no termine mencionando "agentes", "tokens", "LLMs". Términos que manejamos con soltura —yo incluido— sin poder siempre explicar con precisión qué son ni cómo se relacionan entre sí. Se han vuelto vocabulario de oficina tan rápido que dimos por sentado que los entendíamos, cuando en realidad los estamos usando como sinónimos de algo mucho más amplio: "la IA", así, en singular y sin matices. El problema es que "la IA" no es una cosa. Es un campo con 66 años de historia, dos fracasos públicos y sonoros, y una convergencia final de piezas que estuvieron dispersas durante décadas antes de encajar. Entender ese recorrido —de dónde viene cada palabra que usamos hoy— es lo que te permite, después, distinguir con precisión entre inteligencia artificial, machine learning, LLMs y las herramientas que armamos con ellos. Ese es el objetivo de esta serie. Empecemos por el principio. La palabra que se inventó en un verano de 1956 En el verano de 1956, un grupo pequeño de matemáticos e ingenieros se reunió en Dartmouth College, en New Hampshire, convocados por un joven profesor llamado John McCarthy. El objetivo declarado del encuentro —ocho semanas de trabajo, financiadas por la Fundación Rockefeller— era ambicioso hasta rozar lo temerario: explorar la idea de que cualquier aspecto del aprendizaje o de la inteligencia pudiera describirse con tanta precisión que una máquina lograra simularlo. Ahí, en esa propuesta, se usó por primera vez el término "inteligencia artificial". No fue un hallazgo técnico puntual; fue una apuesta filosófica con nombre propio. McCarthy y sus colegas —entre ellos Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon y Nathaniel Rochester— no tenían todavía las herramientas para cumplir esa promesa. Tampoco imaginaban cuánto tiempo iba a tomar. Ese desfasaje entre la ambición del nombre y la capacidad real de la tecnología es, en más de un sentido, el patrón que se repite durante las siguientes seis décadas. Cuando el campo prometió de más, dos veces La historia de la IA no es una línea ascendente. Es una historia de entusiasmo, promesa incumplida, y colapso de financiamiento — dos veces. El primer episodio ocurrió a mediados de los años 70, cuando la Agencia de Proyectos de Investigación Avanzados de Defensa de Estados Unidos (DARPA, por sus siglas en inglés) retiró buena parte del financiamiento a la investigación general en IA, al no ver resultados militares concretos. Un informe británico crítico de la época, el llamado Informe Lighthill, terminó de sellar el desánimo. (Vale una aclaración honesta: entre historiadores del campo hay debate sobre si este "primer invierno" fue tan severo como se suele contar en retrospectiva, o si es una narrativa que se simplificó con el tiempo. El segundo episodio, en cambio, no admite discusión.) Ese segundo invierno llegó a fines de los 80. La industria había apostado fuerte a los llamados "sistemas expertos" — programas que codificaban el conocimiento de un especialista humano en reglas del tipo "si pasa esto, entonces hacé aquello". Funcionaban, hasta que dejaban de funcionar: eran costosísimos de mantener, y una sola regla faltante podía romper el sistema entero. Cuando el hardware especializado que sostenía esa industria se volvió obsoleto frente a estaciones de trabajo genéricas mucho más baratas, el mercado colapsó casi de un día para el otro. Universidades enteras perdieron financiamiento. El término "inteligencia artificial" mismo cayó en desprestigio durante casi una década. Es importante decir esto en voz alta: la IA no fue una marcha triunfal e ininterrumpida hacia el presente. Fue, dos veces, un campo que casi se extingue. El otro camino: aprender de los datos en vez de programar reglas Mientras los sistemas expertos se derrumbaban, un enfoque distinto venía tomando forma en paralelo, casi silenciosamente. En vez de programar reglas explícitas para cada situación, ¿y si un sistema pudiera aprender esas reglas por sí mismo, a partir de ejemplos? Ese enfoque —el aprendizaje automático, o machine learning — no es sinónimo de inteligencia artificial. Es un subconjunto de ella: una familia específica de técnicas dentro del campo más amplio que se inauguró en Dartmouth. Y dentro del machine learning hay, a su vez, un subconjunto más específico todavía: el deep learning , o aprendizaje profundo, que usa redes neuronales de múltiples capas inspiradas —de forma bastante libre— en la estructura del cerebro. Esta relación de contención (IA contiene a ML, que contiene a deep learning) no es un detalle técnico menor. Es, probablemente, la fuente número uno de confusión en cualquier charla de oficina sobre el tema. Cuando alguien dice "la IA hizo esto", casi siempre se está refiriendo a un modelo de deep learning específico — no al campo entero. El problema del deep learning, durante décadas, fue que la teoría existía pero le faltaban dos cosas: datos suficientes para aprender patrones complejos, y poder de cómputo suficiente para procesarlos en un tiempo razonable. Esa carencia se resolvió recién en 2012. Cuatro piezas que estaban dispersas Ese año, un modelo llamado AlexNet ganó por una diferencia abrumadora una competencia de reconocimiento de imágenes llamada ImageNet. No ganó por poco: superó al segundo lugar por casi diez puntos porcentuales de precisión, algo inédito hasta ese momento. La clave no fue solo el diseño de la red neuronal, sino la combinación de dos factores que hasta entonces habían viajado por separado: un dataset masivo de imágenes etiquetadas y el uso de placas gráficas (GPUs) — hasta entonces pensadas para videojuegos, no para entrenar redes neuronales — para paralelizar el entrenamiento. Ese fue el primer encastre. El segundo llegó cinco años después, y fue puramente arquitectónico. En 2017, un equipo de Google publicó un paper con un título casi provocador: Attention Is All You Need . Proponía una nueva forma de procesar secuencias de texto —el Transformer— que abandonaba el procesamiento palabra por palabra a favor de un mecanismo de atención que evalúa todas las palabras de una oración en simultáneo, en paralelo. Esa arquitectura es, hoy, el motor que corre por debajo de prácticamente cualquier modelo de lenguaje que uses: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, todos. El tercer encastre fue una constatación empírica. En 2020, investigadores de OpenAI publicaron evidencia de que la performance de un modelo de lenguaje mejora de forma predecible —siguiendo una ley de potencia— a medida que aumentás su tamaño, la cantidad de datos de entrenamiento y el cómputo disponible. Esto no era obvio de antemano. Antes de este hallazgo, escalar un modelo era una apuesta; después, se convirtió en una fórmula con resultados razonablemente predecibles. Esa confianza fue lo que justificó construir GPT-3, un modelo de 175 mil millones de parámetros que en 2020 validó esas leyes de escala a una magnitud sin precedentes. Y sin embargo, GPT-3 —a pesar de todo ese poder— era torpe para conversar. Estaba entrenado para completar texto, no para responder preguntas ni seguir instrucciones. Ahí entra la cuarta pieza, la que casi nunca aparece cuando se cuenta esta historia en versión corta: una técnica llamada aprendizaje por refuerzo con retroalimentación humana (RLHF), que se usó para afinar el modelo a partir de ejemplos de conversaciones reales, evaluadas y corregidas por personas. Ese ajuste fue lo que en noviembre de 2022 se convirtió en ChatGPT: no un modelo más grande, sino un modelo por fin usable . Llegó a cien millones de usuarios en dos meses — a Instagram le había tomado más de dos años alcanzar esa cifra. Lo que esta historia deja en claro "La IA" que irrumpió en la conversación de oficina en 2022 no apareció de la nada. Es el resultado de 66 años de trabajo, dos colapsos de financiamiento que casi terminan con el campo entero, y una convergencia final de cuatro piezas —datos, cómputo, arquitectura y una técnica de alineación— que existieron por separado durante años antes de que alguien las juntara en un mismo producto. Esa distancia entre "inteligencia artificial" (el campo completo, con 66 años de historia) y "ChatGPT" (una aplicación puntual de una técnica específica, ajustada con otra técnica específica) es exactamente la distancia que se pierde cuando usamos todos estos términos como si fueran intercambiables. Y es el punto de partida para la Parte 2: qué es realmente un LLM, dónde termina el modelo y empieza la herramienta, y por qué esa distinción no es solo semántica — cambia lo que podés esperar, razonablemente, de cada una.
